title: TEDxUCSB Lost My Talk. Here Is What I Did About It. Leadership Empathy Elevated
author: Empathy Elevated
summary: The Empathy Elevated author recounts how TEDxUCSB lost the video recording of their May 2025 talk introducing the PACE System (TM) -- and then used the PACE System itself to navigate nine months of institutional failure and escalating silence from the organizing committee. The talk was the first public presentation of PACE (Pause, Ask, Consider, Empathize), a framework built from thirteen years of watching empathy fail in high-stakes technical environments. The recording was lost because the committee relied on a Facebook livestream that auto-deletes after 30 days, and no one notified the speaker until nine months later when they asked. The author's response -- documenting every channel, distinguishing those with integrity from those with authority, escalating to UCSB administration, and ultimately going public -- models the framework under genuine adversity. The article doubles as a practical guide for speakers: verify recording logistics in writing before signing.
points: The PACE System applies to adversity first: Pause (separate what was lost from what remains), Ask (document every channel before assuming malice or incompetence), Consider (distinguish those with authority from those with visibility), Empathize (extend empathy to future speakers in similar situations).

The fact that the framework designed for high-stakes empathy failures was the tool the author used when their own high-stakes moment failed is a proof of concept: frameworks tested under personal duress carry more credibility than frameworks presented in optimal conditions.

TEDx events are independently organized under license from TED -- the brand is only as good as the local committee, and speakers are entitled to ask organizers directly how they plan to fulfill the recording requirement before signing.

Transparency should have been a notification in June 2025 when the recording was lost -- not a written confirmation nine months later when the speaker finally asked; this failure of proactive communication is the institutional accountability failure at the center of the story.

The credential from a TEDx talk has standalone professional value even without the video -- the work existed, the moment existed -- but speakers are entitled to both the credential and the record, and should secure recording commitments in writing before the event.
quotes: I had prepared not a theory, but a system forged through thirteen years of watching empathy fail in high-stakes technical environments. Now with a name, The PACE System was ready for the stage.

The committee confirmed in writing that the recordings were lost. They relied on a Facebook livestream. They said it auto-deletes 30 days after the event. The committee had since dissolved, and no remedy was offered. They oddly noted they 'wanted to be transparent.' Transparency would have been a notification in June 2025, when the recording was lost, not nine months later, when I asked.

Pause: I did not react the day I found out. I sat with it. I separated out what was permanently lost from what remained intact. I organized my records into a Dropbox. The credential was real. The talk happened. The framework existed independently of the video. The pause was not inaction, but the first move.
Pause. Ask. Consider. Empathize. The system I introduced on that stage is the exact system I used when the stage failed me. I did not plan that. But I will not pretend it isn't a proof of concept.

TEDx events are independently organized under license from TED. The brand is only as good as the local committee. This is not a criticism of TED. It is an explanation of the structure. Before you say yes to a TEDx event or really any event where you are giving your time: ask your organizer directly how they plan to fulfill the recording requirement.

The talk exists. It happened. The PACE System was filed for federal trademark in February 2026. The keynote version of my TEDx talk is ready, and the idea that empathy is the one human advantage AI will never replicate is as relevant today as it was on that stage one year ago.
